name: Adaptive Practice With Regrouping
title: Adaptive Practice With Regrouping
answer: Adaptive practice with regrouping means using AI math software to adjust each problem to a student's last answer, then having the teacher use the software's reports to form small groups for the next day's instruction. It matters because the software gains are real but modest, and the larger improvement usually comes from how teachers act on the data rather than from the program itself.

sections.body: Adaptive practice is the most familiar use of AI in math classrooms, where programs adjust each problem based on how a student answered the previous one. It solves the problem of one-size-fits-all practice by keeping students working at a level that matches their current grasp of a topic. The idea pairs that software with regrouping, in which the teacher reads the reports and pulls together small groups of students who need the same thing next. The software supplies the data and the teacher supplies the instruction, so the tool supports teaching rather than replacing it. This division of labor is what turns modest software effects into something a classroom can actually use.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In elementary grades, programs such as Zearn adjust problems as students work, while older students may use Khan Academy in the same adaptive way. The teacher then looks at what the software reports and forms small groups for the following day. For example, a teacher might pull five students for a short lesson on equivalent fractions while the rest of the class continues practicing. The text describes this pattern across kindergarten through 12th grade rather than giving separate routines for each grade band, so the grouping decision stays with the teacher at every level.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels the evidence for this idea as real but modest. A review of 21 studies of AI in kindergarten through 12th grade math found a small positive effect overall, with larger effects when the software acted as a tutor or adaptive system (Yi et al., 2024). Another review found that intelligent tutoring helped students in general, but the advantage shrank when it was compared with other practice software rather than with no software at all (Letourneau, 2025). A mapping of adaptive learning research found that relatively few systems had been put to work on real student problems in real schools (Kabudi et al., 2021). The text also notes that a tool which works in a research study may work differently in a crowded sixth grade class with patchy internet, and it points to the pilot method in Chapter 4 as the way to find out.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets clear limits on what adaptive practice can deliver. A district switching from one practice program to another should not expect a large jump, because the comparison advantage shrinks when the alternative is other practice software rather than no software at all. The bigger gains usually come from how teachers use what the software reports, so the grouping and instruction decisions stay with the teacher. The mapping finding is a reminder to ask vendors for evidence from classrooms like your own, since a tool that works in a research study may behave differently in a crowded class with patchy internet. The pilot method in Chapter 4 is the text's answer to that uncertainty, and nothing here is legal advice.
